messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Officer Katarina Volkov

Katarina Volkov was thirty-two months into her career with the metropolitan police department when the training scenario went catastrophically wrong. It was meant to be a routine firearms exercise in the basement range—a controlled environment, full safety protocols, her supervising sergeant standing ten feet away. The trainee officer beside her had been certified, or so everyone believed. When his weapon discharged into her abdomen at point-blank range, the impact threw her backward against the cinder-block wall. She remembered the sergeant's face frozen in shock, the acrid smell of cordite, the sensation of her own blood spreading warm across her ribs before the pain arrived. What she remembered most, though—what returned to her unbidden in the weeks that followed—was the moment she realized the weapon had been loaded with live rounds. The trainee had not checked. No one had checked. The people she had trusted to keep her safe had failed her in the most fundamental way.

The physical injuries healed within four months. The bullet had missed her spleen by centimeters; she was told she was lucky. But by the time Katarina returned to light duty in the autumn, something had fractured that no surgeon could repair. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt unshakeable, that her own body was a traitor. Her heart would race without warning—in the grocery store, at a red light, sitting on the couch beside her girlfriend Marcus. Her hands would tremble when she held a coffee cup. Her breathing would shallow and quicken as though her lungs had forgotten how to work. These reactions made no sense to her. She was safe. She was home. Yet her body insisted, moment after moment, that danger was imminent and closing in. What terrified her most was that she could not trust herself anymore. If her body could betray her like this, how could she rely on it to protect her? How could she trust anyone else when the institution she had devoted herself to had failed so catastrophically?

The memories came without warning, vivid and complete. When they arrived, Katarina was no longer in her apartment in November 2024; she was back in that basement range, the fluorescent lights humming overhead, the smell of gun oil and concrete filling her nostrils, the weight of the sergeant's stare. The sensations were so immediate and overwhelming that she would sometimes find herself on the floor, unsure how she had gotten there. What made it worse was that these memories felt profoundly alien to her—as though they belonged to someone else, some other woman who had been shot, not to Katarina herself. She would watch herself in these moments from a distance, seeing her own hands shaking, her own chest heaving, as though observing a stranger in crisis. The detachment was almost as disorienting as the vividness. She could not control when the memories forced their way in. They came while she was driving, while she was trying to sleep, while Marcus was speaking to her and her mind simply vanished into that basement without permission.

Over the following months, Katarina's sense of the world had shifted into something darker and more fragile. The precinct, once a place of purpose and belonging, now felt like a minefield of incompetence and negligence. She was certain that danger lurked in ordinary moments—that the next mistake, the next oversight, the next betrayal by someone she had to trust, was always seconds away. When she returned to full duty in January, she found herself hypervigilant in ways that exhausted her. Every sound in the station made her flinch. Every interaction with her colleagues carried an undercurrent of suspicion. She trusted no one to check equipment, to follow protocol, to keep her safe. This wariness, this conviction that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that people would inevitably fail her, seemed to reach backward and intensify the memories themselves. The more certain she became that danger was omnipresent, the more forcefully the basement memory intruded, as if her mind was trying to prove to her that her fears were justified. The memories and her appraisals had become locked in a vicious cycle: each one feeding the other, each one making the other feel more real, more true, more inescapable.

By October, Katarina had begun avoiding shifts that required her to work in the basement, making excuses to her sergeant that she knew were transparent. She had stopped going to the gun range entirely—a decision that had begun to isolate her from her unit and raise questions about her fitness for duty. Marcus had noticed the withdrawal too, the way Katarina would tense when sirens passed their apartment, the way she had stopped sleeping more than a few hours at a time. When Marcus tried to hold her at night, Katarina would feel her body stiffen, her breathing quicken, as though she were being threatened rather than comforted. She had not told Marcus the full extent of what was happening—the intrusive memories, the sense of unreality, the conviction that her own body was working against her. She was afraid that if she spoke it aloud, it would become even more true. It was only last week, when she had called in sick for the fourth time in two weeks and her lieutenant had asked her directly if she needed to see someone, that Katarina had finally admitted to herself that she could not manage this alone. She had come to her first therapy appointment carrying the weight of a betrayal so complete that she had begun to wonder whether she could ever trust her own mind again.
